faq.a: An Open Market Operation (OMO) sale is when the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sells government securities (bonds) to banks, effectively withdrawing money (liquidity) from the financial system.

faq.q: Why is RBI selling government bonds now?
faq.a: The RBI is selling government bonds to absorb excess liquidity present in the banking system, which helps manage inflation and stabilize short-term interest rates.

faq.q: How will this affect my fixed deposit rates?
faq.a: An OMO sale can lead to a slight hardening of interest rates. Over time, this might prompt banks to offer marginally higher interest rates on fixed deposits to attract funds.

faq.q: Will my home loan EMI change?
faq.a: If you have a floating-rate home loan, a general increase in interest rates due to OMOs could lead to a slight increase in your EMI or loan tenure, depending on your bank's policy. For new loans, the initial rate might be marginally higher.

faq.q: Is this a sign of rising interest rates?
faq.a: An OMO sale to absorb liquidity generally indicates the RBI's intent to manage inflationary pressures and can contribute to a modest upward pressure on interest rates in the short to medium term.

faq.q: What is the difference between OMO sale and OMO purchase?
faq.a: An OMO sale involves the RBI selling government bonds to withdraw liquidity from the system, while an OMO purchase involves the RBI buying bonds to inject liquidity into the system.
